result.summary: Tereus of Thrace, married to Progne, fetches her sister Philomela from Athens, rapes her, cuts out her tongue and imprisons her, then tells Progne that Philomela is dead. After a year Philomela weaves the story into a cloth and sends it to Progne, who reads it and turns toward revenge.

scenes.title: Prologue and Athens unvisited
scenes.summary: A summary of the tale is given, then neighboring Greek cities are listed as visiting Pelops' mourning court, while Athens, at war, alone does not.

scenes.title: The ill-omened wedding
scenes.summary: Tereus drives off the invaders and wins Progne from Pandion in a marriage attended by Furies and an owl. Their son Itys is born.
scenes.stakes: The marriage is doomed from the start.

scenes.title: Tereus desires Philomela
scenes.summary: Progne asks that her sister visit. Tereus sails to Athens, sees Philomela and is consumed by lust, and feigns Progne's wishes to win Pandion's consent.
scenes.stakes: Philomela is unaware that she is in danger from Tereus.

scenes.title: Departure by ship
scenes.summary: After a sleepless night Tereus receives Pandion's tearful charge, and sails away with Philomela, gloating like an eagle with a hare.

scenes.title: Rape and mutilation
scenes.summary: Tereus locks Philomela in a forest dwelling, rapes her, and cuts out her tongue when she threatens to expose him. He lies to Progne that her sister is dead.
scenes.stakes: Philomela's body, voice and life; Tereus fears exposure.

scenes.title: The woven message
scenes.summary: After a year Philomela weaves her story into a web and sends it secretly to Progne, who reads it in stunned silence and plans revenge.
scenes.stakes: Philomela hopes to expose Tereus and be freed; Progne decides to act.

alias_notes.explanation: Gradivus is a title of Mars, the Roman war god.
The Odrysians were a Thracian people, so this names Tereus as king of Thrace.
Titan and Phœbus here both mean the sun god, used to mark the passing of time.

notable_quotes.reason: Ovid's aside on the hidden darkness of human hearts, as Tereus' lust disguises itself as affection.
Famous line that misfortune sharpens ingenuity, introducing Philomela's tapestry.

analysis.text: The tale shows lust and violence silencing a woman, and her answer through art. Weaving becomes speech when the tongue is taken.
The story reflects Greek and Roman stereotypes of Thracians as barbarous. Ovid's irony about omens and appearances is typical of his style.

legacy.text: The myth of Philomela became the classic poetic image of the nightingale's song and lament, used by many later poets, including T. S. Eliot in The Waste Land (1922).

fun_facts.text: Greek and Roman sources disagree on which sister became the nightingale and which the swallow.

language_notes.text: The cities come to console Pelops, whose grief is for his children, the Niobids, killed after Niobe's boast (the preceding tale). The list is a catalogue of Greek places.
"Mopsopian" means Athenian, from Mopsopus, an early legendary king of Attica.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, god of war; Tereus is thus presented as his descendant.
Hymeneus (Hymen) is the god of weddings; his absence signals a marriage without divine blessing.
The Furies, avenging goddesses, carry funeral-pyre torches instead of wedding torches, perverting the marriage ritual.
The owl was a Roman bird of ill omen, often linked with death and disaster.
Titan here is the Sun (Hyperion's son), whose yearly course measures time; 'five autumns' means five years have passed since Progne's marriage.
Cecropian means Athenian, from Cecrops, legendary first king of Athens.
Joining right hands was the formal gesture of greeting and pledge; 'evil omen' means the talk began under inauspicious signs.
Naiads are water nymphs and Dryads tree nymphs, the female spirits of nature, proverbially beautiful.
'The people in those regions' refers to Thracians, whom Roman writers stereotyped as passionate; Tereus is king of Thrace.
The narrator exclaims that human hearts hide dark secrets, as night hides things; 'dark night' means concealed wickedness.
'By her own safety (and against it too)' is ironic: she swears by her safety, which this very journey will destroy.
Phœbus is the sun god driving his chariot; his steeds descending Olympus' track means sunset is near.
Odrysian refers to the Odrysae, a Thracian people; Tereus is king of Thrace.
The bird of Jupiter is the eagle, the king of the gods' sacred bird and his traditional emblem.
Supplanter means one who takes another's place; Philomela says she has displaced her sister as Tereus's wife in effect, while he is husband to both.
Conscious rocks means rocks that can be aware and bear witness, so her voice would reach even them.
The twice six signs are the twelve zodiac signs; the sun passing through them marks one full year.
Warp is the set of vertical threads on a loom; she sets up the loom and weaves her story into cloth.

context_notes.text: This summary is a later heading, not Ovid's own words; it gives away the whole plot of Tereus, Progne and Philomela.
Thrace, in the north Aegean region, was regarded by Greeks as wild and warlike, which suits Tereus' later violence.
Progne is daughter of Pandion, king of Athens, and wife of Tereus of Thrace; her sister Philomela remains in Athens.
The Piræus was Athens' port, a few miles from the city.
Tereus considers bribery or abduction followed by war, showing he is already planning to seize Philomela by force.
Pandion, king of Athens, is entrusting Philomela to Tereus so she can visit her sister Progne, Tereus's wife in Thrace.
Progne exchanges bright robes for black mourning dress and builds an empty tomb, a cenotaph, for the sister she thinks dead.

literary_notes.text: The narrator's startled question stresses how surprising and shameful Athens' absence is.
Addressing Athens directly adds reproach and draws the reader into the narrator's emotion.
The Furies and the owl at the wedding point ahead to the crime, vengeance and horror of the tale.
The festivals celebrate days that bring disaster, so the narrator's moral comment underlines the couple's blindness to their fate.
The 'evil omen' warns that this meeting will end in catastrophe.
Lust is compared to fire in dry grain and leaves, suggesting quick, destructive spread.
The narrator suddenly addresses the gods, stressing moral horror at Tereus' hidden deceit.
Tereus is praised as affectionate for the very deceit that conceals his crime.
Philomela rejoices at what the narrator says will bring sorrow; the reader knows more than she does.
Pandion's shuddering at the presages of his own mind hints that the journey will end in disaster.
Tereus is compared to an eagle with a captured hare, casting Philomela as helpless prey.
The wounded lamb and bloodied dove convey her lingering terror and vulnerability after the attack.
The severed tongue is likened to a snake's writhing tail, a gruesome image that makes it seem alive and seeking its owner.
A general maxim about grief and ingenuity prepares for the weaving of the message.
Progne, who needs words most, is struck silent; the cloth speaks where spoken language has been taken away.
